en_revised: He arrived at the city of Jayapura (闍耶補羅城) and stayed at a temple of the non-Buddhists (外道寺). The temple was located outside the western gate of the city, and at that time his companions numbered more than twenty people.

issues: the country of Rājya (礫迦國) → 礫迦 is the Life's form of 磔迦, Ṭakka (Xiyu ji 04.01; Beal: the kingdom of Tcheka (Takka)); DM's “Rājya” misnames the country; it is time for you all to know this → 諸人宜共知時: all of you should know that now is the time [to give] (Beal: an opportunity for adding to … merit)
en_revised: The next day, he arrived at the eastern border of the country of Ṭakka (礫迦國, i.e. 磔迦) and reached a large city. To the west of the city and north of the road was a large mango grove, in which lived a Brahman seven hundred years old; yet when one looked at him, he appeared to be only about thirty, with a stalwart physique and a profound, discerning mind, being well-versed in the *Madhyamaka* and *Śata* treatises and proficient in the *Vedas* and other such books. He had two attendants, each over one hundred years old. The Master met with him, and he received the Master with great joy. Having also learned that the Master had been robbed, he immediately dispatched an attendant to order the Buddhist laypeople in the city to prepare food for the Master. In the city there were several thousand households; those who believed in Buddhism were few, while those who followed non-Buddhist paths were very numerous. When the Master was in Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅), his reputation had already spread far and wide and was known to all countries; the messenger then went throughout the city and announced: "The monk from the land of China (支那國) has arrived; he was robbed by bandits nearby and all his clothes are gone; all of you should know that now is the time [to give]." Moved by the power of his merit, the heretical parties reformed their hearts; more than three hundred prominent people, upon hearing the news, each brought a piece of patterned cotton cloth along with food and drink, arriving respectfully to pile them before him, bowing and kneeling to inquire after his well-being. The Master offered blessings for them and explained the retribution of cause and effect, causing all those people to generate the intention for the path, abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox, and they returned home laughing, talking, and dancing with joy. The aged man sighed that this was something that had never happened before. Thereupon, he distributed the patterned cotton cloth among the various people, and each received enough for several sets of clothing, with still more left over; he then offered fifty bolts of cloth to the aged man. He remained there for one month to study the *Śata-śāstra* (經百論) and the *Śata-śāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論). That person was a disciple of Nāgārjuna (龍猛) who had received the teachings directly from his master, and his explanations were exceptionally clear and pure.

issues: Iranaparvata (伊爛拏) → Īraṇa[parvata] (伊爛拏), the Life's short form of 伊爛拏鉢伐多; name form as in the Xiyu ji translation (10.01: Īraṇaparvata)
en_revised: Several tens of yojanas from the southern border of the country, there is a great mountain forest, dense and lush, stretching for more than two hundred li. Within it, there are many wild elephants that roam in herds of several hundred; therefore, the two countries of Īraṇa[parvata] (伊爛拏) and Campā (瞻波) have the most elephant troops, as they frequently order elephant trainers to capture and tame them in this forest for national use. It is also abundant in jackals, rhinoceroses, and black leopards, so no one dares to travel there.  Tradition says that before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was a cowherd tending several hundred cows who drove them into the forest. One cow would leave the herd and go off alone, often disappearing to an unknown place, but when it was time to return at sunset, it would rejoin the herd with a beautiful, radiant luster and an extraordinary lowing that terrified the other cows, none of whom dared to stand before it. After many days of this, the cowherd wondered at the cause and secretly waited to watch it; in a moment the cow left again, and he followed to observe it. He saw the cow enter a hole in the rocks and followed it inside; after about four or five li, it suddenly opened into a bright expanse where the woods and fields were magnificent, filled with many strange flowers and fruits so brilliant they dazzled the eyes, unlike anything seen in the common world. The cow ate grass in one place, the color and fragrance of which were also unknown in the human world. The man saw that the fruit trees were yellow-red like gold, fragrant and large, so he picked one; although his heart was greedy for it, he was still afraid and did not dare to eat it. After a while the cow came out and the man followed it to return, but when he reached the aperture in the rocks and had not yet emerged, an evil demon snatched the fruit and kept it. The cowherd asked a great physician about this and described the appearance of the fruit. The physician said that it should not be eaten immediately, but that he should find a way to bring one out. The next day, he again followed the cow inside and picked one fruit, intending to bring it back in his bosom, but the demon again blocked him to snatch it. The man put the fruit into his mouth, and when the demon gripped his throat, the man swallowed it. Once the fruit entered his stomach, his body became enormous; although his head could get out, his body remained stuck in the hole, and he could not return. His family went searching for him and, seeing his transformed form, were all struck with fear, yet he was still able to speak and explain what had happened. His family returned and summoned many strong men to pull him out together, but they could not move him at all. The king heard of this and came to see for himself; fearing it might become a future calamity, he sent men to dig and pull, but they also could not move him. As months and years passed, he gradually turned into stone, though he still retained a human shape. Later, another king, knowing that he had been transformed by a divine fruit, said to his attendants: "Since his body was transformed because of the medicine, his body itself is the medicine; although it looks like stone, its substance is ultimately divine, so we should send someone to take a small piece with a hammer and chisel." The attendants obeyed the king's command and went with craftsmen, exerting all their strength to carve and chisel, but after ten days, they could not obtain even a single piece, and it remains there to this day.
